paragraphs.heading: What counts as a small body
paragraphs.text: A small Solar System body is an object in the Solar System that is not a planet, not a dwarf planet and not a natural satellite. The International Astronomical Union (IAU) first set out the term in 2006, as a shared label for every other object going around the Sun apart from moons. So the group takes in all comets, and all minor planets except the dwarf planets.

paragraphs.heading: Who belongs
paragraphs.text: In practice that means the comets, the classical asteroids other than Ceres, which is a dwarf planet, the trojans, the centaurs and trans-Neptunian objects. Pluto, Eris, Haumea, Makemake and several other dwarf planets are left out of the group. So is any body that may later turn out to be a dwarf planet.

paragraphs.heading: Born with Pluto's demotion
paragraphs.text: The definition came from the same 2006 IAU resolution that defined the word planet and moved Pluto down to the rank of dwarf planet. Read in context, it covers every object orbiting the Sun that is not a planet or a dwarf planet. Visitors from beyond the Solar System do not count. Interstellar objects passing through, such as 1I/ʻOumuamua, 2I/Borisov and 3I/ATLAS, are excluded.

paragraphs.heading: Moons and borderline cases
paragraphs.text: Apart from the largest moons, which are in hydrostatic equilibrium, moons are not told apart from small bodies by size but by orbit. A moon circles a planet, a dwarf planet or even a small body, not the Sun. Some of the larger small bodies may be moved into the dwarf planet class later, once further study shows whether they are in hydrostatic equilibrium. There is also no agreed lower size limit yet. It is not clear whether the class will one day reach all the way down to meteoroids, the smallest macroscopic bodies that orbit the Sun.

paragraphs.heading: Where they live
paragraphs.text: Most small bodies orbit in two zones, the asteroid belt and the Kuiper belt. Each belt has some inner structure shaped by the tug of major planets, above all Jupiter for the asteroid belt and Neptune for the Kuiper belt, and neither has sharp edges. Smaller groups turn up in other parts of the Solar System too. These include the near-Earth asteroids, the centaurs, the comets and the scattered disc objects.
